standard: RFC 9449 §10.1, taken in by FAPI 2.0 §5.3.2.1 item 12
text: An AS accepts the DPoP key from the PAR request's DPoP header alone
behaviour: `dpop_jkt` is required in the signed JAR. A DPoP header on PAR must match it; a header alone is refused
why: With the header alone, a compromised Front reposts the RP's JAR with its own key's header, binds T to the attacker's key, and gets both the victim's token and the key it is bound to (Tamarin `PAR_DPOP_HEADER_ONLY`)

text: Members of a claims request that are not understood MUST be ignored
behaviour: The direct members of `id_token` and `userinfo` written as null are read as `{}` (the same meaning). Any other null in `claims` is refused with 400 `invalid_request_object`, at PAR for a pushed request and at /login/start for one by value
why: The statement T the person approves is signed whole, and the signer writes no null (OIDC Core §13.3). A part of the request that cannot be signed as given is refused before the person is asked, never silently dropped from what they approve

text: `dpop_jkt` is an optional authorization request parameter; FAPI does not require the client to send it
behaviour: A JAR without `dpop_jkt` is refused
why: When the Front relays the token request, binding the authorization to the RP's DPoP key in the signed request is what keeps a compromised Front from redeeming the code under its own key (claim 1)

text: A confidential client's refresh token need not be bound to the DPoP key; FAPI names rotating the key without losing the grant as a benefit
behaviour: A confidential client's refresh family is bound to the authorization's DPoP key; a refresh under another key is refused
why: A family not bound to the key can be refreshed by whoever holds the token, including a compromised Front that saw it (claim 2)

text: An AS may accept `authorization_details`
behaviour: `authorization_details` is refused at PAR and on every grant at the token endpoint
why: Per-operation authorization belongs to the RS and 4s-intent, not the IdP (V6); accepting it would make the IdP decide operations

text: The Security Profile accepts an authorization request without a signed request object
behaviour: Every authorization request is a signed JAR (PAR in a FAPI configuration, F4)
why: Without a signed request, a compromised Front rewrites the request the person approves (claim 1's code-grant hole). Applies only if the Security Profile plan is run

standard: RFC 6749 §4.1.2; OAuth 2.0 Multiple Response Type Encoding Practices §2.1; RFC 9207; FAPI 2.0 Security Profile
text: An AS may return the authorization response in the redirect URI's query, made safe by `iss` (RFC 9207); the client may leave `response_mode` out
behaviour: A JAR must carry `response_mode=form_post`; the response is a POST to the redirect URI, never its query
why: Against login CSRF: the RP's callback takes the response by `form_post` alone and checks that its `Origin` is exactly the login screen's, its `state` cookie `SameSite=None; Secure`, so a response another site sends the victim's browser is refused

text: A request object may leave `jti` out
behaviour: A JAR without `jti` is refused; one JAR starts one login, held by its client and `jti` until its expiry and the clock skew
why: The Core uses one JAR, and its `request_uri`, for one statement T alone, which needs the JAR named

text: A client should send `typ` `oauth-authz-req+jwt` (FAPI 2.0 Message Signing); the AS need not require it
behaviour: A JAR without `typ` `oauth-authz-req+jwt` is refused; the type is compared as a media type, without case
why: Explicit typing keeps a JWT made for another purpose with the same client key from being passed off as a request object

text: An AS refuses a request object whose `exp` is more than 60 minutes after its `nbf`
behaviour: PAR refuses a JAR whose `exp` is further than its own `jar-max-lifetime` (90 seconds by default) from the time it takes it; the login's start checks it again against `authorize`'s
why: A short `exp` and the Core's own cap keep long-lived JARs from piling up reservations

text: `state` is recommended, not required; in FAPI 2.0, PKCE gives the protection against CSRF that `state` gave
behaviour: A JAR without `state` is refused
why: The RP binds `state` to the browser session and redeems no response it did not begin; the login screen takes the redirect's `state` from the signed T, so a request without it leaves the RP nothing to hold the response to (login CSRF)

text: `nonce` is optional in the authorization code flow
behaviour: A JAR without `nonce` is refused, whether or not it asks `openid`
why: The ID token's `nonce` ties it to the RP's own request: one of the checks that keep a login in the browser session that asked for it

text: An AS that uses a `request_uri` once is recommended to spend it at the point of authorization, not when the authorization page is loaded
behaviour: The same JAR with the same screen keys is answered the same T; a second start with other screen keys (a reloaded screen has new ones) is refused, even before the person authenticates
why: The JAR's reservation binds it to one statement T and one screen's keys from its first start; a second T for the same JAR would let a compromised Front have an attacker approve it on another screen and swap that code into the victim's session (login CSRF)

text: `login_required` for `prompt=none` is an authentication error response, returned to the client at its redirect URI
behaviour: A pushed request asking `prompt=none` is refused at PAR with 400 `login_required`; a request by value is refused at /login/start the same way. No T is issued
why: Every login asks the person's passkey, so `prompt=none` is never met; PAR may answer an error itself, which tells the RP at its own server, with no round trip through the browser and no redirect the Core does not authenticate

text: `state` and `nonce` have no length limit
behaviour: A `state` or `nonce` longer than 512 bytes of UTF-8 is refused with 400 `invalid_request`, at PAR and at /login/start
why: T, the statement the person approves, carries both and must fit its route to the screen (4096 characters); 512 each leaves room for a long client, redirect URI, scope and `claims`. The OIDF suite's 1000-character `state` is refused, which it marks a warning

standard: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 §15.1; OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 §3 (`id_token_signing_alg_values_supported`)
text: OPs MUST support signing ID tokens with RS256, unless they return ID tokens from the token endpoint alone and let clients register only `none`; `id_token_signing_alg_values_supported` MUST include RS256
behaviour: The recommended configuration signs ID tokens with ES256 alone, and the metadata names that algorithm alone. An operator may set the authority ring to RS256 (warned of at every start as deprecated), which then meets the RS256 requirements of §15.1 and Discovery §3, and no longer FAPI 2.0 §5.4.1. The standards conflict here: FAPI 2.0 leaves RS256 out
why: FAPI 2.0 Security Profile §5.4.1 allows PS256, ES256 and EdDSA alone, and nextgen takes FAPI 2.0 with ES256 signing. Serving both would need a key per algorithm and a choice of algorithm per client (not held: V29)

text: Servers SHOULD support RS256 for client assertions at the token endpoint, and SHOULD support `none` and RS256 for request objects
behaviour: Client assertions and request objects are taken under ES256, PS256 and EdDSA by default; RS256 only where the operator names it, warned of at every start. `none` is never taken, and an unsigned request is refused (`jar-required`)
why: FAPI 2.0 Security Profile §5.4.1 allows PS256, ES256 and EdDSA alone

text: A client assertion's audience SHOULD be the URL of the authorization server's token endpoint
behaviour: A client assertion's `aud` is taken as the issuer identifier, a string, alone: the token endpoint's URL, or a list, is refused. A registered client may be set to take a loose audience (`accept-loose-audience`), a weakening choice warned of at every start: claim 2 is judged not to hold
why: FAPI 2.0 Security Profile §5.3.2.1 asks the issuer alone, as a string: an assertion made for another server cannot be taken here (claim 2)

standard: OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 §3 (`userinfo_endpoint`); OpenID Connect Core 1.0 §5.4
text: `userinfo_endpoint` is RECOMMENDED; when an access token is issued, the claims of the `profile`, `email`, `address` and `phone` scopes are returned from the UserInfo endpoint
behaviour: The recommended composition offers no UserInfo endpoint (`userinfo` is opt-in); the claims of the scopes asked are released in the ID token. Composing `userinfo` is a weakening choice: claims 1 and 2 are judged not to hold
why: A UserInfo answer is bound to neither the token it was asked with nor the request, so a compromised Front can replay an older answer of wider attributes, or answer any `sub` it likes

text: A client's keys may be given by reference at its `jwks_uri`, which is preferred over the inline `jwks` for easier key rotation
behaviour: In the recommended composition a client's keys are those written in its record alone: a registry record naming a `jwks_uri` has no key, and nothing is fetched for it; a client written in the configuration may name one only as a weakening choice, which the promise judgment reports as breaking claim 2
why: Keys fetched from a URL rest on whoever serves it and on the fetch's TLS, not on the publisher's signed registry, so claim 2 would depend on them

text: `userVerification` defaults to `preferred`, at a key's creation and at each authentication: the Relying Party may take a response without the UV flag
behaviour: Passkey ceremonies ask `userVerification: "required"`, and a response without the UV flag is refused. Any other `passkeys` `user-verification` setting breaks the promise of a new login
why: A new login is the person's own approval of the request with their passkey, every time (D6); user verification (fingerprint, face or PIN) makes the tap the person's, not only someone's presence

text: Relying Parties that wish to support a wide range of authenticators SHOULD include at least -8 (EdDSA), -7 (ES256) and -257 (RS256)
behaviour: Creation offers ES256 and EdDSA by default (`webauthn.algorithms`); RS256 only where the operator names it, warned of at every start. An RS256 passkey already registered is still verified
why: RS256 signs by PKCS#1 v1.5, which the provider leaves out of every default where it signs or verifies, warning of it as deprecated; a 2048-bit RSA key holds about 112-bit security

text: A DPoP proof is signed by a key the client chooses; it is tied to the client's authentication only by sharing its TLS connection, a cryptographic binding being left out of scope
behaviour: client_credentials (opt-in, a weakening choice) takes `private_key_jwt` by a key written in the client's registry record alone, and its DPoP proof must be by that same key, the token's `cnf`; a proof by another key is refused `invalid_dpop_proof`
why: TLS ends at the Front, so a compromised Front could pass the client's assertion on and swap the proof for one by its own key, getting a token bound to the attacker's key in the client's name (claim 2; Tamarin `CC_PROOF_ANY_REGISTERED`)

text: The authorization server MUST ignore unrecognized request parameters; every OP MUST support enforcing `max_age`, and `display`, `ui_locales`, `claims_locales` and `acr_values` must at least not result in an error
behaviour: A JAR naming any item outside the login's closed set is refused (`unknown_item`, `invalid_request_object`): `max_age`, `display`, `ui_locales`, `claims_locales`, `acr_values`, `login_hint` and `id_token_hint` among them, until a decision adds one
why: The statement T the person approves is signed whole and compared exactly, its items one closed set; an item the screen neither checks nor shows could be added or changed by a compromised Front, so none is carried that is not named

text: Scope values used that are not understood by an implementation SHOULD be ignored; the authorization server may fully or partially ignore the scope requested, by its policy
behaviour: A login's `scope` naming a value outside the client's allowed scopes, an unknown one among them, is refused `invalid_scope` (RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1: the scope requested is invalid, unknown or malformed) at the push and at the start; no value is dropped
why: T is written from the RP's signed request as given, and the person approves its scope exactly (O14); a value the Core will not carry is therefore refused before the person is asked, never dropped, so the RP is not issued less than it signed for without being told (this row's consequence of O14)

text: An authorization request that fails for a reason other than a missing or invalid redirect URI is answered to the client at its redirect URI, the error in the response
behaviour: A login's start refused before its statement T exists (a reload or a second tab under other screen keys, a `request_uri` unknown, spent or expired) shows the error on the login screen's own page and sends the browser nowhere; the person starts again at the RP
why: Before T the screen holds no redirect URI the Core checked (under PAR, none at all), so sending the browser to one would be an open redirect (RFC 9700 §4.11.2)

text: An RSA COSE key's modulus is 2048 bits or larger, applications may restrict its length further, and the public exponent is not restricted
behaviour: An RS256 passkey's key is taken with a modulus of 2048 to 4096 bits and the public exponent 65537 alone; any other is refused
why: Bounded keys keep each verification's cost known, as RFC 8230 §6.1 advises checking a key's length to limit the resources it takes
